title: Aram and Damascus
lead: Aram was the land of the Arameans in Syria; its strongest kingdom, centered on Damascus, was Israel's great rival in the ninth century BC under kings called Ben-hadad and Hazael. The patriarchs' kin came from Aram, and Aramaic, its language, became the common tongue of the Near East.

sections.b: Israel remembered Aramean roots: "My father was a wandering Aramean" (Deuteronomy 26:5), and Laban lived in Aram (Genesis 25:20). David defeated Aramean kingdoms (2 Samuel 8:3–8; 2 Samuel 10), and Rezon founded a hostile kingdom in Damascus in Solomon's time (1 Kings 11:23–25). In the ninth century Ben-hadad of Damascus fought Ahab (1 Kings 20; 1 Kings 22), Elijah was told to anoint Hazael (1 Kings 19:15), and Elisha met Naaman and Hazael (2 Kings 5; 2 Kings 8:7–15). Hazael's wars nearly destroyed Israel (2 Kings 10:32–33; 2 Kings 13:3–7). Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC (2 Kings 16:9). Assyrian inscriptions name Hadadezer and Hazael of Damascus, and the Tel Dan Stele is probably Hazael's.
